items.title: Who is accountable for what (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK, How government works; Managing Public Money; Civil Service Code
items.body: Accountability means being answerable for what you do, and having to explain and justify it to someone else. In central government the chain runs as follows. Ministers are accountable to Parliament for the policies and actions of their department. They can be questioned in the House of Commons and by parliamentary committees, and in serious cases they can be pressed to resign. Civil servants are accountable to their ministers, and through them to Parliament. They advise and carry out decisions, but it is the minister who answers publicly for the department's policy. In each department the Permanent Secretary is also the Accounting Officer. This is a personal responsibility to Parliament for how the department spends public money. The Accounting Officer must make sure money is used with regularity (within the rules and the law), propriety (to high standards of conduct), value for money and feasibility. If a minister wants to do something that the Accounting Officer thinks breaks these tests, the Accounting Officer can ask for a written instruction from the minister, called a ministerial direction. The department's accounts are then examined by the National Audit Office. Understanding this chain helps you see why records are kept and why decisions need to be explained. Public servants spend other people's money, so they must be able to show how and why it was spent.

items.title: How Parliament checks the government (level 3)
items.source: UK Parliament website; National Audit Office
items.body: Parliament does two main jobs. It makes laws, and it checks, or scrutinises, the government. There are several ways in which MPs and peers check what departments are doing. In the House of Commons, ministers answer oral questions at set times, and the Prime Minister takes questions each week. MPs can also table written questions, and ministers must reply on the record. A reply may contain facts and figures about a department's work, and civil servants usually draft it. Select committees are small groups of MPs from different parties. Each one watches a particular department or topic. For example, the Work and Pensions Committee examines the Department for Work and Pensions. Committees hold inquiries, call ministers and senior civil servants to give evidence, and publish reports with recommendations. The Public Accounts Committee looks at how well public money has been spent and often works with the reports of the National Audit Office. Departments must reply to committee reports within a set time. Civil servants who give evidence to a committee do so on behalf of their minister and tell the truth. MPs also raise their constituents' problems with departments, and each department has a team that handles letters from MPs. This is why accuracy and prompt replies matter in everyday work.

items.title: Special advisers (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK, Special advisers; Code of Conduct for Special Advisers
items.body: Not everyone who works for a minister is a politically impartial civil servant. Special advisers, often called spads, are a different group. They are appointed by a minister to help with the political side of the job. They might help write speeches, deal with party matters, or give the minister advice on how a decision will be seen by the public. Special advisers are temporary civil servants. Their appointments end when the minister leaves office or at the next general election. They are not appointed on merit through open competition, and they are not required to be politically impartial. This is allowed by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010. However, they are bound by their own Code of Conduct. Special advisers must not take actions that need an impartial civil servant, such as managing permanent civil servants. They also cannot authorise the spending of public money. They must follow the rules on honesty and integrity, and they must not misuse official resources. The reason for the arrangement is that it keeps party politics separate from the permanent Civil Service. The minister can get political support from the special adviser, while the civil servants stay impartial. If a civil servant is asked for political work, they should raise it with their manager, since it is not their job.

items.title: Official information and the right to ask (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK, Freedom of Information; Official Secrets Act 1989; Civil Service Code
items.body: Civil servants handle a lot of information that is not for public use, so they need to understand the rules. The Official Secrets Act 1989 makes it a criminal offence for current and former Crown servants to disclose certain categories of information without authority, such as information about security, defence or international relations. Many civil servants are told about it when they join. The Civil Service Code also says civil servants must not disclose official information without authority, and that duty continues after they leave. But government is also expected to be open. The Freedom of Information Act 2000 gives anyone the right to ask a public authority for information it holds. The authority must normally reply within 20 working days. It will either supply the information or explain why it can't, for example because it would reveal personal data, harm national security, or damage the government's ability to give advice freely. Anyone can make a request, and they do not have to give a reason. Authorities also publish a lot of information proactively. When an FOI request arrives, the rule is that it should be passed to the department's FOI team, who will deal with it. A civil servant should not decide alone what can be released. Ask your manager if unsure.

items.title: Looking after personal data (level 3)
items.source: Information Commissioner's Office; UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018
items.body: Personal data is any information that can identify a living person, such as a name, address, date of birth, National Insurance number, bank details, health information or a photograph. The law that protects it is the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR), together with the Data Protection Act 2018. The independent regulator is the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The law sets principles for handling data. It must be used lawfully, fairly and openly. It must be collected for a clear purpose and not used for something unconnected. Only what is needed should be collected. It must be accurate and kept up to date. It should not be kept longer than necessary. And it must be kept secure. In practice this means civil servants should only look at records they need for their work, check they are sending information to the right person, use official systems and not personal email, lock their screen when they leave their desk, and never take customer information home without authority. People have rights over their data. They can ask to see what is held about them, which is called a subject access request, and they can ask for mistakes to be corrected. If personal data is lost or sent to the wrong person, this is a data breach, and it must be reported to your manager or the data protection team straight away. Delay can make things worse.

items.title: The centre of government (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK, Cabinet Office; HM Treasury; Cabinet Manual
items.body: Some parts of government help to run the whole system. The Prime Minister leads the government, appoints the other ministers and chairs the Cabinet. The Cabinet Office supports the Prime Minister and the Cabinet, and it helps departments work together. It also looks after the Civil Service as a whole. For example it publishes guidance for civil servants and runs central services. The Cabinet Secretary is the most senior civil servant in the Cabinet Office. They are the Head of the Civil Service and give advice to the Prime Minister on how government should be run. The Cabinet Secretary also leads the civil servants who serve the Cabinet. HM Treasury is the government's economic and finance ministry. It sets taxes and public spending plans and agrees how much each department can spend. The Chancellor of the Exchequer is the minister who leads the Treasury, and the Chancellor presents the Budget to Parliament. Departments must get Treasury approval for big new spending. 10 Downing Street is the Prime Minister's official home and office, and 11 Downing Street is the official residence of the Chancellor. Together, the Prime Minister's team, the Cabinet Office and the Treasury are known as the centre of government. They set the framework in which departments operate.

items.title: Non-ministerial departments and agencies (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies
items.body: Government organisations come in several types, and it helps to know what they are called. A ministerial department is led by a minister, such as the Home Office and the Ministry of Justice. A non-ministerial department is also a full government department, but it is not led by a minister day to day. Examples include HM Revenue and Customs, the Food Standards Agency, Ofsted and the Competition and Markets Authority. HMRC is led by a board chaired by a senior official, and the Treasury minister who is responsible answers for it in Parliament. Non-ministerial departments often have a regulatory or inspection role, where operating at a distance from ministers helps them show that decisions are fair. An executive agency is a part of a department with a clear task, and it is usually led by a chief executive. It has a framework document that sets out its aims and how much freedom it has. This approach became widespread after a reform programme in the late 1980s, which was called Next Steps. Examples include the DVLA, HM Passport Office and HM Land Registry. Executive agencies employ civil servants and follow the Civil Service Code. When you read an advert, check whether the employer is a department, an agency or an arm's length body, because the job and the organisation's culture may differ.

items.title: Where the Civil Service came from (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK, History of the Civil Service; Northcote-Trevelyan Report
items.body: Until the 19th century many government jobs in Britain were given out through patronage, which means that people got posts because of who they knew, not because of what they could do. In 1853 the government asked Sir Stafford Northcote and Sir Charles Trevelyan to look at the way the service was organised. Their report, published in 1854, is now known as the Northcote-Trevelyan Report. It set out ideas that still shape the Civil Service. It said that civil servants should be recruited by open competition, tested by examination and appointed on merit, instead of through patronage. It said there should be a permanent, politically neutral service that could serve whatever government was in power. And it said that people should be promoted on their performance. The reforms were adopted over time. A Civil Service Commission was set up in 1855 to run the examinations. In 2010 the Commission was given a legal basis by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act, which also put the principles of the Civil Service in law. Today's four values of integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality are the modern form of those ideas. The history explains why recruitment is fair and open, and why civil servants stay when governments change.

items.title: Grades and what they usually do (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK, Civil Service grades; Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Grades give a rough guide to the level of responsibility in a job, though what the job involves differs between departments. An Administrative Assistant (AA) does basic office and support tasks, such as filing, scanning, sorting post and entering simple data, under close guidance. An Administrative Officer (AO) does more varied and responsible work. That often involves processing claims or cases, answering enquiries, checking documents and updating records. An Executive Officer (EO) has more responsibility. EOs might handle more complex cases, check work done at AO level, lead a small team or take on tasks that need judgement. A Higher Executive Officer (HEO) often manages a team or leads a project. HEOs might supervise EOs and AOs, advise on how rules should apply, or work on policy analysis. A Senior Executive Officer (SEO) manages managers, or leads a specialist area. Grade 7 and Grade 6 are senior roles that lead larger teams and work with senior leaders. Above these is the Senior Civil Service (SCS), which begins at Deputy Director level and includes Directors, Directors General and Permanent Secretaries. The AO job you apply for is one step on a ladder. Knowing the next step helps you plan how to build the skills and experience needed for promotion.

items.title: Early career routes (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK, Civil Service Fast Stream; Civil Service apprenticeships
items.body: There are several routes into the Civil Service, and they suit different people. The most common is to apply directly for a vacancy on Civil Service Jobs at AA, AO or EO level. This route is open to people with all kinds of backgrounds and qualifications, and it is the usual way in for someone starting without a degree. The Civil Service Fast Stream is a graduate development programme. It is designed to prepare people for senior roles, and it involves a series of placements in different parts of government. Entry is competitive and normally needs a degree, and applications run on set dates each year. Apprenticeships are another route. An apprentice is employed and paid, works in a real job and studies towards a recognised qualification at the same time, usually with time off for study. Apprenticeship levels range from the equivalent of GCSEs to degree level and beyond, and the Civil Service offers them in areas such as business administration, digital, finance, project management and customer service. There are also schemes for particular groups, such as internships for students and programmes for disabled people. People can move between routes later in their career, for example by taking an apprenticeship after joining. The best route depends on your qualifications, your goals and how quickly you want to start earning.

items.title: Functions, professions and GOV.UK (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK, Civil Service functions and professions; Government Digital Service
items.body: Because the Civil Service is so large, it organises specialist jobs into functions and professions that cover the whole of government. A function is a group of people who do a particular kind of work across departments and share standards and training. Examples include Finance, Commercial (buying goods and services), Digital, Data and Technology, Human Resources, Communications, Project Delivery, Property and Security. A profession is similar but based on a recognised skill set. Examples include the Government Legal Profession, the Government Economic Service, the Government Statistical Service and the Government Social Research profession. These bodies help civil servants to learn, share good practice and move between departments. The Government Digital Service (GDS) is part of the Cabinet Office. It builds and runs GOV.UK, the single website where people find information and services from across government. GOV.UK replaced hundreds of separate websites when it launched in 2012. GDS also sets standards for how digital services should be designed. Civil Service Jobs itself is an example of a shared service used by all departments. When you apply for a job, the advert tells you the profession or function, and joining one can open a route to a long-term career with specialist training.

items.title: Treating people fairly: the Equality Act (level 3)
items.source: Equality Act 2010; Equality and Human Rights Commission; GOV.UK
items.body: The Equality Act 2010 is the law that protects people from discrimination. It applies to employers and to organisations that provide services, so it covers both how the Civil Service treats its staff and how civil servants treat the public. The Act lists nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. Discrimination means treating someone worse because of a protected characteristic. Direct discrimination is when someone is treated less well for that reason. Indirect discrimination is when a rule that seems to apply to everyone puts people with a protected characteristic at a disadvantage. The Act also requires reasonable adjustments for disabled people, to remove barriers so they are not at a disadvantage. In addition, public bodies must follow the Public Sector Equality Duty. This means that when they make decisions, they must think about the need to remove discrimination, advance equality of opportunity and foster good relations between different groups. In daily work this means treating every customer with respect and giving everyone the same quality of service. It also means offering help, such as a different way to contact the department, to customers who need it, and challenging unacceptable behaviour. The Equality and Human Rights Commission is the body that enforces the law.

items.title: Handling complaints about services (level 3)
items.source: GOV.UK, complain about a government department; Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
items.body: Things sometimes go wrong, and people have a right to complain about a government service. Departments publish their complaints procedures, and staff should know how to recognise and pass on a complaint. Most departments handle complaints in stages. At the first stage the person's complaint is looked at by the team or a complaints team, who try to put things right and reply in writing. This may include an apology, an explanation or a correction of a mistake. If the person is still not satisfied they can ask for a review by someone more senior in the department. After that, some organisations have an independent body that looks at complaints. Examples are the Independent Case Examiner for the Department for Work and Pensions and the Adjudicator's Office for HMRC. If the complaint is still not resolved, the person can ask their MP to refer it to the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman, an independent officer who investigates complaints about UK government departments and the NHS in England. Complaints are valuable because they show where services need to improve. When someone complains to you, listen without arguing, apologise if the department got it wrong, say what happens next and make sure the complaint is recorded. A complaint is not a personal attack, and it should never be ignored.

items.title: Security classifications and handling information (level 3)
items.body: The government marks information according to how sensitive it is, so people know how carefully to handle it. The system is called the Government Security Classifications. There are three levels. OFFICIAL covers most of the information that civil servants deal with. It includes day-to-day work such as case records, policy drafts and correspondence. It is not for public release, but its loss would cause limited damage. Some OFFICIAL information is especially sensitive, such as personal data or commercial information, and can be marked OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE, which is a handling instruction rather than a separate level. SECRET is for very sensitive information that could seriously harm national security, the safety of individuals or major operations if lost. TOP SECRET is for the most sensitive information, where compromise could threaten national security on a large scale. Most Administrative Officers work only with OFFICIAL material. Good handling habits apply to everything. Do not leave documents or screens where others can see them. Lock your computer when away. Use approved systems and equipment, not personal email or messaging apps, to send work information. Check the address before you press send. Report any loss of papers, devices or passes straight away. Security rules protect people as well as information, so they are not red tape.
